Poverty and Test Performance in New York Public Schools

Charlie Ma

2026-09-21

library(tidyverse)
library(knitr)
merged <- read_csv("data/processed/nys_merged.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(poverty_group = factor(poverty_group, levels = c("low", "medium", "high")))

tbl <- function(x) read_csv(paste0("output/tables/", x, ".csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)

Question

What does the data say about poverty and test performance in NY public schools — how big is the gap, is it closing, and does free/reduced lunch access change it?

Data: nys_schools.csv (one row per school-year, 2008–2017, NYS Education Department) and nys_acs.csv (one row per county-year, 2009–2016, American Community Survey).

What I did

1_clean.R

  • Recoded -99 to NA. It appears in both numeric and character columns, so each type needs its own na_if().
  • Dropped 24 exact duplicate rows, and 19 rows that were -99 in every field but the school name.
  • Kept the 1,725 rows with a missing district_name — those are charter schools, which have no district. Dropping them would lose most of NYC.
  • Set per_free_lunch / per_reduced_lunch to NA where they exceed 1 (44 rows, max 257) or sum above 1 (42 rows). The two are mutually exclusive tiers of the same enrollment, so the sum can’t exceed 100%.
  • Split counties into terciles of poverty rate (low ≤ 11.7%, medium 11.7–14.4%, high > 14.4%), pooled across years. Poverty clusters between 11% and 15%, so round cutoffs would empty the middle group; pooling keeps “high poverty” meaning the same thing in 2009 and 2016.
  • Converted scores to z-scores within year. The state changed its test in 2013 (max ELA ~720 → ~355), so raw scores aren’t comparable across years.

Result: 35,620 rows.

2_transform.R — left_join on county_name and year. County alone fans each school-year across all 8 ACS years (284,960 rows). Left rather than inner keeps 2008 and 2017 usable for school-level questions.

3_analyze.R / 4_plot.R — summary tables and the two figures below.

About 0.67 SDs between high- and low-poverty counties, near-identical in ELA and math. The extremes are wider: Bronx −0.77, Nassau +0.88. Tompkins is the exception — 4th-highest poverty but above average, because Cornell grad students inflate its poverty rate, which is a warning that county poverty is a rough proxy.

Q2: Has it changed over time?

kable(tbl("gap_by_year"), digits = 3, caption = "Mean ELA z-score by tier, and the high-low gap")
Mean ELA z-score by tier, and the high-low gap
year low medium high gap
2009 0.440 0.019 -0.530 0.970
2010 0.418 0.027 -0.502 0.920
2011 0.379 0.022 -0.417 0.796
2012 0.425 0.021 -0.393 0.818
2013 0.446 -0.037 -0.220 0.665
2014 0.385 -0.068 -0.153 0.537
2015 0.363 -0.050 -0.142 0.505
2016 0.332 -0.141 -0.101 0.433

The gap halved, from 0.97 SDs in 2009 to 0.43 in 2016, almost entirely because high-poverty counties improved (−0.53 → −0.10) rather than low-poverty counties slipping. Two caveats: the 2013 test change sits inside this window (though the yearly changes are even throughout, so it isn’t an artifact), and z-scores measure relative position only — this shows the distribution compressing, not absolute learning gains.

# Fit the school-level relationship separately in each poverty tier: if lunch
# access moderated the effect, these slopes would differ.
merged |>
  filter(!is.na(poverty_group), !is.na(per_free_reduced), !is.na(mean_ela_score_z)) |>
  group_by(poverty_group) |>
  group_modify(~ {
    fit <- lm(mean_ela_score_z ~ per_free_reduced, data = .x)
    tibble(slope = coef(fit)[2], r_squared = summary(fit)$r.squared, n = nrow(.x))
  }) |>
  kable(digits = 3, caption = "Slope of ELA z-score on free/reduced lunch share")
Slope of ELA z-score on free/reduced lunch share
poverty_group slope r_squared n
low -2.671 0.539 8275
medium -2.382 0.483 6688
high -2.351 0.328 11742

No. The slopes are near-identical across tiers (−2.7, −2.4, −2.4), so lunch access doesn’t soften the poverty relationship — it measures the same disadvantage better, explaining 46% of score variance on its own (pooled; the per-tier figures are in the table above). Within high-poverty counties alone, low- vs high-lunch-access schools differ by 1.21 SDs, nearly twice the entire between-county gap.

This is eligibility, not treatment — the variable counts students who qualify for assistance, so it proxies family poverty. Nothing here says anything about whether the meals help; every eligible student presumably receives them, so the data contains no variation in access to measure.

Takeaway

The gap is large (0.67 SDs) and closing (0.97 → 0.43). But county poverty is the wrong targeting variable: school-level lunch share predicts performance better, is already collected, and identifies struggling schools inside wealthy counties that a county-level measure would miss.

Limitations

  • Correlational. Lunch access, county poverty and scores are all downstream of the same conditions.
  • County poverty is assigned to every school in the county, which isn’t where poverty actually varies.
  • School mean scores hide within-school variation.
  • Z-scores are relative, so convergence can’t be separated from a test that spreads schools less widely.
  • 2,208 ELA scores are missing; if smaller or poorer schools are likelier to be missing, these gaps are understated.
  • 2008 and 2017 drop out of county analyses for lack of ACS data.
  • Poverty tiers are assigned per county-year, and 38 of 62 counties change tier at some point, so the groups compared in Q2 are not a fixed set of counties.
